subject: history
subTopic: Analysing Sources: Origin, Purpose, Value and Limitation

questions.content: A historian is told to state the ORIGIN of a source. Which answer gives the origin?
options: Who created it, when and where
Why the author wanted to persuade
Whether the content is true
What the source cannot tell us
questions.explanation: Origin means who made the source, when and where. Purpose is why it was made, and limitation is what it cannot tell us.

questions.content: Which of these is a PRIMARY source for the study of a war fought in 1916?
options: A school textbook written in 2015
A soldier's letter home written in 1916
A documentary film made in 1998
A museum website written last year
questions.explanation: A primary source was created at the time by someone involved or present. The other three were produced long afterwards.

questions.content: A government poster from the 1910s shows a brave soldier and the words 'Your country needs you'. What is the most likely PURPOSE of the poster?
options: To record casualty figures accurately
To give a neutral account of the war
To persuade men to join the army
To entertain people at home
questions.explanation: Recruitment posters were made by governments to persuade. Their purpose shapes what they show, so they are not neutral records.

questions.content: What is a SECONDARY source?
options: Any source that is less important than another
Any source that is shorter than a book
A source written by someone who disagrees with the government
A source produced later by someone who was not there, usually by studying other evidence
questions.explanation: Secondary sources are produced after the event by people such as historians who study evidence. They are not 'second best'.

questions.content: A student says, 'This source is biased, so it is useless.' What is the best response?
options: Correct, biased sources should be ignored
Biased sources can still be valuable, for example to show what the author or government wanted people to believe
Only primary sources can be biased
Bias only matters in newspapers
questions.explanation: Bias is not the end of the analysis. A biased source can reveal attitudes, propaganda aims and the views of a group, which is real value.

questions.content: Read this invented extract. 'Diary of Marta Kessel, factory worker, 3 March 1871: The new machines run from dawn to dusk. My hands are cracked and we are fined for being a minute late. Yet the wage keeps my brother in school.' A student writes that the diary has high value for studying daily life in a factory. What is the best justification?
options: It was written by a worker who experienced the conditions at the time
It was written by a historian using many sources
It proves that all factories were the same
It was written many years later as a memoir
questions.explanation: Value comes from the author's first-hand experience at the time. It would be a mistake to claim it proves all factories were the same.

questions.content: Using the same invented diary of Marta Kessel (a factory worker, 1871), which is the best LIMITATION of the source?
options: It is a primary source
It records only one worker's experience in one place, so it may not be typical
It was written in 1871
It mentions wages
questions.explanation: A limitation is what the source cannot tell us. One diary cannot show the experience of all workers, and a primary source and a date are not limitations.

questions.content: An invented newspaper editorial from 1898 is titled 'Our Navy Guards the Seas of Freedom'. It was printed in a paper owned by a shipbuilding company. Which question would best help a historian judge its reliability?
options: How many pages did the newspaper have?
Could the owner's business interests have shaped what was written?
Is the title in capital letters?
Was the newspaper printed in black ink?
questions.explanation: Origin includes who owned or paid for the source. A shipbuilder has a financial reason to praise naval spending, which affects reliability.

questions.content: A historian is studying how ordinary people reacted to a new law. She finds an official government report, a private letter from a farmer and a speech by a minister. Which approach is best?
options: Use only the government report as it is official
Use only the farmer's letter as it is private
Compare all three and note how each author's position and purpose shape their view
Choose the longest source
questions.explanation: Cross-referencing sources and considering each author's position gives a more balanced judgement than relying on any one source.

questions.content: An invented photograph from 1932 shows smiling villagers receiving food parcels from officials. The caption was written by the government press office. What can a historian reasonably say about its VALUE?
options: It proves the villagers were happy with the government
It is worthless because photographs can be staged
It shows how the government wanted its relief work to look, though it may not show typical experience
It must be accurate because it is a photograph
questions.explanation: A staged or selected image still tells us about government image-making. It cannot be treated as proof of general feeling, but it is not worthless either.

questions.content: Which pair correctly matches a source with a sensible question about PURPOSE?
options: A private diary: who paid for it to be printed?
A recruitment poster: what response did the government want from viewers?
A statistics table: what colour is the paper?
A history textbook: was the author alive at the time?
questions.explanation: Purpose asks what the creator wanted the source to achieve. For a poster the aim is a response from viewers such as joining up or buying bonds.

questions.content: A student is asked to 'evaluate the value and limitations of a source'. Which answer best matches the command term?
options: List three facts from the source
Copy the source in your own words
Make a judgement by weighing what the source offers against what it cannot show, using origin and purpose
State the date of the source
questions.explanation: Evaluate means to make a reasoned judgement by weighing strengths and weaknesses. Listing or describing alone earns little credit.

questions.content: An invented letter from 1850, written by a mill owner to a magistrate, says, 'The children in my mill are well fed and happy.' A historian says the letter has little value for judging working conditions. A second historian says it has real value. Which reasoning best supports the SECOND historian?
options: The letter proves the children were well fed
The letter shows how an employer defended his mill to the authorities, which helps explain the debate about child labour
Letters are always reliable
A mill owner always tells the truth
questions.explanation: The letter is weak evidence of real conditions, but it is useful evidence of how employers justified themselves, depending on the question being asked.

questions.content: A source is a 1920 memoir by a retired general describing a battle he commanded in 1915. He writes that his orders were perfect and that failure was caused by others. Which judgement is most convincing?
options: High value as a primary source because he was present, but its reliability is reduced by the time gap and his motive to protect his reputation
No value because memoirs are always lies
High value because generals always have full information
No value because it was written after 1915, so it is a secondary source
questions.explanation: A memoir is still a primary source because the author was involved, but the delay and the author's self-interest limit reliability. The best answer balances both.

questions.content: Two invented sources describe the same strike. Source A, a union leaflet, says 5,000 workers marched peacefully. Source B, a police report, says 800 rioters attacked property. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Source A is correct because unions represent workers
Source B is correct because police reports are official
Both were produced by groups with an interest in the outcome, so the figures differ and the truth needs further evidence
The strike did not happen
questions.explanation: Both sources have a purpose and a position that shape their claims. A careful historian looks for further independent evidence rather than choosing a side.

questions.content: A student argues, 'A secondary source is always less useful than a primary source.' Which counter-argument is strongest?
options: A secondary source can combine many primary sources and show long-term patterns that no single participant could see
Secondary sources are always accurate
Primary sources can never be wrong
Secondary sources are always newer so they are better
questions.explanation: Usefulness depends on the question. A historian's study can draw on many sources and place events in context, which one eyewitness cannot.

questions.content: An invented Ministry of Information film from 1941 shows cheerful crowds queuing calmly after an air raid. A historian wants to use it to study morale. Which approach shows the strongest historical thinking?
options: Accept the film as an accurate record of morale
Reject it because it is propaganda
Use it to show the image the ministry wanted to promote, then test its claims against diaries, letters and private surveys
Ignore the film and use only secondary sources
questions.explanation: Propaganda is valuable evidence of official aims. Corroborating it with independent primary sources lets the historian judge how far morale really matched the image.

questions.content: A source's content is accurate on every checked fact, yet a historian still says it has limited value for her question about public opinion. Which is the most likely reason?
options: Accurate sources are never useful
The source was written by a single official about government decisions and says nothing about what the public thought
The source contains dates
The source was kept in an archive
questions.explanation: Value is always relative to the question. An accurate source can still be limited if it does not address the topic being studied.

note:
## Why sources matter
History is built from evidence. A source is anything that tells us about the past: a letter, poster, photograph, speech, statistic, film or a historian's book. Strong answers do not just say what a source says. They judge how far it can be trusted and how useful it is for a particular question.

## Primary and secondary sources
- **Primary source**: created at the time by someone who took part or witnessed events, such as a diary, law, speech or photograph.
- **Secondary source**: created later by someone who was not there, usually using other evidence, such as a textbook or documentary.
- Neither type is automatically better. A diary gives first-hand feeling but only one view. A historian's book may see the whole picture but depends on the evidence the writer chose.

## OPVL: the four lenses
- **Origin**: Who made it? When and where? What was their position, nationality, job or experience?
- **Purpose**: Why was it made? To inform, persuade, entertain, justify, warn or recruit? Who was the audience?
- **Value**: What does it help us understand? Value is always about a specific question. Even a biased source can be valuable because it reveals attitudes or what a government wanted people to believe.
- **Limitation**: What can it NOT tell us? Is it one person's view? Was it written long after the event? Does it leave out important groups?

## How to write a strong source answer
1. Quote or refer to specific details from the source.
2. Link each detail to origin or purpose, using a sentence like 'This is valuable because the author was present, but limited because...'.
3. Compare with other sources or your own knowledge. If two sources disagree, ask why, not just which is right.
4. Reach a judgement that answers the question set.

## Worked example
Imagine an invented letter from 1915 written by a soldier named Tomas to his mother: 'We are well fed and in good spirits.' Origin: a soldier, 1915, writing to family. Purpose: to reassure his mother, and the letter may have been read by army censors. Value: it shows what soldiers chose to say and the morale they wished to display. Limitation: it may hide real hardship, and it is one man's experience. A historian would check it against his later letters or diaries by others.

## Common mistakes
- Saying a source is 'biased' without explaining how or why it matters.
- Saying 'it is a primary source so it is reliable'. Primary does not mean accurate.
- Writing generic limitations like 'it only gives one side' without linking to the source's details.
- Listing OPVL in four separate paragraphs instead of using them to answer the question.
- Confusing reliability (can it be trusted?) with usefulness (can it help with this question?).

## How this is examined
In the eAssessment you are usually given one or two short sources with a context line, then asked a command-term question such as 'state', 'explain' or 'evaluate the value and limitations of Source A for a historian studying...'. Early parts ask you to pull out information. Later parts need a judgement that uses origin and purpose, and sometimes a comparison of two sources. Always tie your judgement to the specific question.

Exam tip: When you evaluate, never stop at 'it is biased'. Add 'which means...' and explain what the historian can still learn.

flashcards.back: Who created the source, when and where, and what their position or experience was.
Why the source was created and who it was meant for, for example to inform, persuade, justify or recruit.
What the source helps a historian understand about a specific question, even if it is biased.
What the source cannot tell us, such as other viewpoints, missing groups or events after it was made.
Evidence created at the time by someone who took part or witnessed events, for example a diary, speech or photograph.
Something produced later by someone who was not there, usually based on other evidence, such as a textbook.
No. Bias can reveal attitudes, propaganda aims and the views of a group. Explain what it shows rather than dismissing it.
Reliability asks if a source can be trusted. Usefulness asks if it helps answer this particular question. A source can be one without the other.
Make a reasoned judgement by weighing strengths against weaknesses, using evidence such as origin and purpose.

subject: history

questions.content: In history, what is a CAUSE?
options: A factor that helped bring about an event
The date of an event
A result that happens afterwards
A source describing an event
questions.explanation: A cause is a reason why something happened. Results that follow an event are consequences.

questions.content: Which of these is a CONSEQUENCE of the invention of the printing press in the 1400s?
options: The events that led to its invention
The earlier shortage of paper
A faster spread of ideas and printed books
The dates on which presses were made
questions.explanation: A consequence comes after an event. Faster spreading of printed ideas was a result of the press.

questions.content: A long-term cause of a war is best described as
options: a factor that built up over many years
the single event that started the fighting
the first battle
the peace treaty
questions.explanation: Long-term causes develop over years or decades, such as rivalry between states. The immediate spark is a short-term trigger.

questions.content: What is a TRIGGER in a causation question?
options: A long-term trend
A speech by a historian
A map of the area
A short-term event that sets off a crisis already prepared by deeper causes
questions.explanation: A trigger is the immediate event that sets things in motion. It usually only matters because long-term causes already existed.

questions.content: Which statement best describes SIGNIFICANCE in history?
options: How old an event is
How important an event was, judged by its impact, its scale and how long its effects lasted
How many sources exist about it
How many people attended it
questions.explanation: Significance is a judgement about importance: how many people were affected, how deeply and for how long.

questions.content: An invented town, Harlow Bay, saw a fishing industry collapse in 1890 after a new railway brought cheap imported fish. Within ten years, half the population had moved away and a new factory opened. Which is a long-term consequence?
options: The railway being built
The cheap imported fish arriving
The fishing industry collapsing in 1890
Change in the town's economy as a factory replaced fishing
questions.explanation: The railway and imports are causes and the collapse is the main event. The changed economy in the following decade is a longer-term consequence.

questions.content: A student says, 'The assassination of a ruler caused the war.' A stronger answer would be
options: The assassination was the only cause
The assassination triggered a war that long-term tensions between powers had made likely
Wars never have causes
The assassination happened before the war so it must be the main cause
questions.explanation: Good causation answers distinguish triggers from underlying causes and explain how they link. Coming first in time does not make something most important.

questions.content: Which pair is an example of causes that are INTERLINKED?
options: Famine led to unrest, and the unrest made the government spend more on its army, which increased taxes and deepened the famine
Two events happening in different countries with no connection
A cause and its date
A source and its author
questions.explanation: Causes are interlinked when they affect each other. Showing connections between factors is a mark of a high-level answer.

questions.content: A teacher asks you to 'explain the consequences' of a new law on farmers in an invented country. Which response best fits the command term?
options: List the date and name of the law
Describe the farmers' clothes
State who wrote the law
Describe several effects and explain how and why the law led to each, including short-term and long-term effects
questions.explanation: Explain means giving reasons and showing how one thing led to another. A strong answer separates short-term and long-term effects.

questions.content: Historians sometimes rank causes. Which approach to deciding the MOST important cause is strongest?
options: Pick the cause you read about first
Pick the cause that happened last
Judge which cause was necessary for the event to happen, and explain why the others depended on it or were less powerful
Pick the cause with the longest name
questions.explanation: A reasoned ranking uses criteria, such as whether the event could have happened without that factor. Just listing or ordering by time is not a judgement.

questions.content: In an invented country, two events took place: a poor harvest in 1930 and a new tax in 1931. Riots broke out in 1932. A student says the poor harvest was clearly the most important cause because it came first. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing, earlier causes are always more important
Timing alone does not show importance, so the student must explain how much each factor contributed
Harvests cannot cause riots
Riots only happen after taxes
questions.explanation: Chronological order is not a measure of importance. The student must link each factor to the outcome and weigh them.

questions.content: Which event is MOST likely to be called historically significant by the criterion of 'long-lasting impact'?
options: A local fair held for one weekend with no lasting effect
A change in law that reshaped how land was owned for the next hundred years
A rumour that was soon forgotten
A speech heard by ten people
questions.explanation: Significance is strengthened by how long and how widely effects last. A law that shapes life for generations scores highly.

questions.content: Two students argue about an invented revolt. Student A says it was significant because 40,000 people took part. Student B says it was significant because it led to a new constitution that lasted a century. Which statement best evaluates their arguments?
options: Only Student A is right as numbers are the only measure
Only Student B is right as laws are the only measure
Both use valid criteria, scale and lasting impact, and the strongest answer would weigh them and say which matters more for the question
Neither can be right because significance cannot be judged
questions.explanation: Significance can be argued on several criteria. The best response compares criteria and reaches a reasoned judgement.

questions.content: A historian claims that without the invention of a new loom, an invented region's textile boom 'would never have happened'. Which line of reasoning best tests this claim?
options: Check whether other factors such as cheap coal, available workers and overseas demand could have produced the boom without the loom
Count the pages in the historian's book
Assume the claim is true because the loom came first
Ignore the claim as an opinion
questions.explanation: Testing a claim of necessity involves considering alternative explanations and whether the outcome could happen without that factor.

questions.content: Which statement shows the difference between a cause and a condition?
options: They are the same thing
Conditions are always short-term triggers
A condition, such as widespread poverty, makes an event possible, while a cause, such as a particular decision, actively brings it about
Causes are always economic
questions.explanation: Conditions create the background in which events can happen. Causes and triggers are the actions and events that actually produce them.

questions.content: An invented empire collapsed in 1750. A historian lists: weak army, huge debts, a bad harvest, and a rival's invasion. She argues debts were the key cause because they made the army weak and left no money for harvest relief. What kind of argument is this?
options: A random list
A description with no judgement
A claim about causes that are interlinked, with one factor treated as underlying the others
A statement about consequences only
questions.explanation: She links the factors and says one explains the others. This is a causal chain argument, which is a high-level approach.

questions.content: Which sentence is the best conclusion to the question 'How far was the harsh winter the main cause of the army's defeat?' (invented case)?
options: The winter was cold.
The winter was important because it killed horses, but poor supply lines and weak leadership had already left the army unable to cope, so the winter was a trigger rather than the main cause.
The army lost.
Winters always cause defeat.
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion answers 'how far', weighs the named factor against others and reaches a supported judgement.

questions.content: A student must judge whether an invented 1880s strike had short-term or long-term significance. The strike ended after two weeks with no pay rise, but within thirty years unions in the whole country were legal and powerful, partly inspired by it. Which judgement is best?
options: It had no significance because it failed
It had little short-term success but strong long-term significance by inspiring later change
It was significant only because it lasted two weeks
Significance cannot be judged for failed strikes
questions.explanation: Events can fail in the short term and still matter greatly over time. Considering both timescales is a key skill.

note:
## Three big ideas
Every history question asks you to think about why things happened (causation), what happened afterwards (consequence) and how much it mattered (significance). These three ideas appear in nearly every unit you study, from the Industrial Revolution to the Cold War.

## Causation
A **cause** is a reason why an event happened. Good historians do not give a simple list. They sort, link and weigh causes.
- **Long-term causes**: build up over years, such as rivalry between states, poverty or new ideas.
- **Short-term causes**: happen closer to the event, such as a decision or a crisis.
- **Trigger**: the final event that sets things off. It usually matters only because deeper causes already existed.
- **Conditions**: the background that makes an event possible, for example widespread hunger or weak government.
- **Interlinked causes**: factors that affect each other, such as hunger leading to protest, which leads to harsh policing, which increases anger.

To rank causes, ask: could the event have happened without this factor? Did other causes depend on it? Was it the most powerful, or only the most visible? Being first in time does not make something most important.

## Consequence
A **consequence** is a result of an event. Sort them to show depth:
- **Short-term** or **long-term**.
- **Political, economic, social, cultural, environmental**.
- **Intended** or **unintended**. A new law may have an effect nobody planned.
- Effects on different groups. Something helpful to factory owners may harm workers.

## Significance
**Significance** is a judgement about how important an event, person or development was. Useful criteria are:
- **Scale**: how many people were affected?
- **Depth**: how deeply did it change lives?
- **Duration**: how long did the effects last?
- **Relevance today**: does it still shape our world?
Significance depends on perspective. A battle may be vital to one nation and barely noticed by another, and historians change their minds over time.

## Worked example
Question (invented): 'Explain why the mining town of Dunmere declined after 1920.' A basic answer says the mine closed. A better answer says: long-term, the coal seam was running out and cheaper foreign coal arrived. The trigger was the owner's decision to close the mine in 1924. Consequence: unemployment rose, shops closed and young families left. These factors link, because falling demand made the owner close the mine, and closure caused the population to fall. The answer then judges that falling demand was the most important cause since the mine could not have stayed profitable without it.

## Common mistakes
- Writing a list of causes with no links between them.
- Treating the trigger as the only cause.
- Describing events when asked to explain.
- Saying something was 'very important' without a criterion.
- Mixing up causes (before) and consequences (after).

## How this is examined
Questions begin with a context or source and use command terms such as 'state', 'explain', 'discuss' and 'to what extent'. Higher marks need links between causes, a ranking with reasons and a clear judgement. Significance questions ask you to use criteria and compare different views.

Exam tip: For 'how far' or 'to what extent' questions, always weigh at least two factors against each other and finish with a clear, reasoned judgement.

flashcards.back: A factor that builds up over many years before an event, such as rivalry, poverty or new ideas.
A short-term event that sets off a crisis. It matters because deeper causes already existed.
Causes that influence each other, forming a chain. Showing the links is a sign of a high-level answer.
Short-term effects appear soon after an event. Long-term effects develop and last over years or generations.
Intended effects are what people planned. Unintended effects are results nobody expected.
A judgement about how important something was, using criteria such as scale, depth, duration and relevance.
Ask if the event could have happened without it, whether other causes depended on it, and how powerful it was.

flashcards.front: Is the first cause the most important?
flashcards.back: No. Being earlier in time does not make a cause more important. You must explain its contribution.
Weigh a factor against others and give a reasoned judgement about how far a statement is true.

subject: history

questions.content: What is an HISTORICAL INTERPRETATION?
options: A copy of a primary source
A list of dates
A translation of a document
An explanation of the past that a historian builds from evidence and argues for
questions.explanation: An interpretation is a reasoned account of the past. Different historians can reach different interpretations from the same evidence.

questions.content: Why can two historians reach different conclusions about the same event?
options: They choose, weigh and read the evidence differently, and may ask different questions
One of them must be lying
History has no evidence
Only one of them uses sources
questions.explanation: Historians select and emphasise evidence differently and are influenced by their questions and the time they write in.

questions.content: Which word best describes a person's point of view shaped by their role, background and beliefs?
options: Chronology
Perspective
Statistic
Archive
questions.explanation: Perspective is how someone sees events based on who they are and what they experienced.

questions.content: A historian writing in 1950 and another in 2020 disagree about an event of 1800. Which factor might explain the difference?
options: The event changed in the meantime
Historians never use evidence
New evidence, new questions and changing values over time
Dates are not fixed
questions.explanation: Interpretations change as new sources are found and as each generation asks new questions.

questions.content: Which of these is a perspective, rather than a fact?
options: The factory opened in 1840
The factory employed 300 workers
The factory stood beside the river
The factory was the best thing that ever happened to the town
questions.explanation: 'The best thing that ever happened' is a judgement that depends on whose view is taken. The others can be checked.

questions.content: Read this invented extract. 'Textbook of the Republic of Valmar, 1960: Our nation's armies marched into the valley to bring peace to a lawless land.' A neighbouring invented nation's textbook of 1960 says: 'Valmar's armies invaded our valley and seized our farms.' Which explanation best accounts for the two accounts?
options: Both countries' textbooks present the same event from the viewpoint of their own nation, shaped by national interest
One textbook is a primary source and one is not
The event did not happen
Textbooks cannot be compared
questions.explanation: The same event is described in different words because each author represents a national perspective. Comparing them reveals this.

questions.content: A historian claims that 'ordinary women's experience was ignored in most histories written before 1970'. This is an example of
options: a primary source
an interpretation about how historians' focus has changed over time
a statistic
a trigger
questions.explanation: The claim is about how the choice of focus in history writing has shifted. It is an interpretation of historiography, the way history has been written.

questions.content: Two invented historians discuss why the town of Eastmoor rebelled in 1810. Historian X stresses high bread prices. Historian Y stresses a new tax on salt. What is the best way for a student to evaluate the two views?
options: Accept whichever is written first
Reject both
Check what evidence each uses, whether they can both be partly right, and which explains the timing and the places involved better
Choose the shorter argument
questions.explanation: Evaluating interpretations means testing them against evidence and considering whether they can be combined, not just picking one.

questions.content: Which sentence best explains why PERSPECTIVE matters when using a source about a conquest?
options: Conquerors and conquered people often experienced the same events differently, so each account tells us something and leaves something out
Only the conqueror writes history
Perspective is only about the date
Perspective is the same as accuracy
questions.explanation: Both viewpoints are partial. Using several perspectives builds a fuller picture.

questions.content: An invented book published in 1925 praises a king as 'the saviour of the nation'. A 2005 biography of the same king says he cut wages and jailed critics. A student must explain the difference. Which answer is the strongest?
options: One of them must have made up the king
The older book was written when official praise was expected and critics could be jailed, while the newer author could use hidden records and was free to criticise
The 2005 book is always right because it is newer
The 1925 book is always right because it is older
questions.explanation: The best answer connects each interpretation with its context, the evidence available and the freedom to write. Newer is not automatically better.

questions.content: A student writes: 'This historian only gives one view, so the interpretation is wrong.' What is the best improvement?
options: Repeat the same point more strongly
Explain what the interpretation emphasises, what it leaves out, and whether the evidence supports its claims
Say all historians are wrong
Say the historian is too old
questions.explanation: Evaluating an interpretation means assessing its use of evidence and balance, not dismissing it for having a viewpoint.

questions.content: Which situation shows a change of interpretation because of NEW EVIDENCE?
options: A historian changes the colour of a book cover
A historian simply feels differently about the event
A student reads a different chapter
Historians re-evaluate a ruler after secret letters are discovered showing he tried to prevent a war
questions.explanation: Newly found sources can change what historians argue. A change of mood or format is not a change in evidence.

questions.content: A historian writes a history of a war using only memoirs written by generals. What is the most likely effect on her interpretation?
options: It will be free of any viewpoint
It will include every group's experience equally
It will emphasise leaders' decisions and may overlook the experience of ordinary soldiers and civilians
It will be fully accurate because generals knew everything
questions.explanation: The choice of evidence shapes an interpretation. Relying on one type of source tends to reproduce that group's viewpoint and leave others out.

questions.content: A historian argues that an invented empire's rule 'brought roads and schools, so it was good for its people'. A second historian argues it 'took land and silenced local languages, so it was harmful'. Which approach shows the strongest historical thinking?
options: Say empires are always good
Say empires are always bad
Ask who benefited and who lost, over what time, and which evidence supports each claim, then give a balanced, justified judgement
Pick the historian who is more famous
questions.explanation: Strong analysis avoids simple verdicts. It looks at different groups, timescales and evidence and reaches a supported conclusion.

questions.content: A student must compare two invented interpretations of a famine. One blames drought and the other blames government exports of grain. What would be the most convincing way to judge between them?
options: Look for evidence of whether food was exported while people starved, and whether earlier droughts had caused famine on this scale
Choose the one with the more emotional language
Choose the one with fewer pages
Believe both equally with no further thought
questions.explanation: Testing each claim against specific evidence, including comparisons with other cases, allows a reasoned judgement.

questions.content: A museum in an invented country removes a display about a massacre carried out by its army in 1890 and replaces it with a display about the army's bravery. What is the best historical comment on this change?
options: It proves the massacre never happened
It shows that how a past event is presented can depend on present-day political aims
It has no importance for historians
It shows that museums are primary sources of the 1890 event
questions.explanation: The museum's choices are an interpretation shaped by present purposes. It tells us about the museum's context, not necessarily about 1890.

questions.content: Which of the following BEST distinguishes an interpretation from propaganda?
options: An interpretation never has a viewpoint
Propaganda always uses numbers
Propaganda is always older
An interpretation is argued from evidence and can be tested and challenged, while propaganda aims to persuade by selecting or distorting evidence
questions.explanation: Both can have a viewpoint, but interpretations rest on open reasoning with evidence. Propaganda sets out to persuade with a hidden or distorted selection.

questions.content: A student writes: 'Historian A says the king was weak. Historian B says he was strong. Both are partly right because he was strong in war but weak in managing money.' What skill is shown?
options: Copying a source
Avoiding the question
Describing without evidence
Evaluating interpretations by recognising that they can focus on different aspects and be combined
questions.explanation: The student sees that disagreements may come from emphasising different aspects, and builds a more complete judgement from them.

note:
## What is an interpretation?
The past is gone, so we reconstruct it from evidence. An **interpretation** is a historian's reasoned account or explanation of the past. It is not just a collection of facts. It is an argument built on selected evidence, for example 'the revolt happened mainly because of food prices'. Because evidence is incomplete and historians ask different questions, interpretations can differ.

## Why do interpretations differ?
- **Different evidence**: historians may use different sources, or new sources may be discovered.
- **Different emphasis**: one historian highlights economic causes, another highlights ideas or leaders.
- **Different questions**: a historian studying soldiers will see a war differently from one studying civilians.
- **Time and context**: each generation has its own values and concerns. Histories written under a strict government may praise it, while later historians may criticise it.
- **Nationality and group**: people from different countries or groups can see the same event differently.
- **Purpose**: some accounts are written to teach, to persuade or to justify a policy.

## Perspective
**Perspective** is how a person or group sees events based on their role, experiences and beliefs. During a conquest, a ruler, a soldier, a local farmer and a merchant will all describe it differently. None of them is the whole truth. Historians put perspectives together to build a fuller picture. Recognising perspective is different from saying someone is lying.

## Fact, opinion and judgement
- A **fact** can be checked ('the factory opened in 1840').
- An **opinion** or **judgement** depends on the person ('it was a great success').
- Interpretations mix facts with judgements, so ask how far the facts support the judgement.

## How to evaluate an interpretation
1. Identify the main claim in your own words.
2. Say what evidence supports it and what it leaves out.
3. Consider who wrote it, when and why.
4. Compare it with another interpretation. Are they really opposed or do they emphasise different aspects?
5. Make a judgement about which is more convincing and why.

## Worked example
Two invented historians discuss why the Kingdom of Orlan lost a war in 1790. Historian A says weak generals lost it. Historian B says a shortage of grain starved the army. To evaluate, check: does evidence show orders ignored or bad battle plans (supporting A)? Did soldiers desert due to hunger (supporting B)? You might conclude both mattered and that hunger weakened the army so generals had little chance, so B explains more.

## Common mistakes
- Saying one interpretation is wrong just because it differs.
- Assuming newer interpretations are always better.
- Confusing an interpretation with a primary source.
- Describing what each historian says without comparing or judging.
- Treating perspective as another word for lying.

## How this is examined
You may be given two short extracts from historians or two accounts of the same event and be asked to compare, explain differences, or evaluate which is more convincing. Higher marks come from linking differences to evidence, context and purpose, and from reaching a judgement.

Exam tip: When explaining why two accounts differ, name a specific reason, such as author, date, audience or emphasis, and show it using details from the extracts.

flashcards.front: Can a newer interpretation be worse?
flashcards.back: Yes. Newer is not automatically better. It depends on the quality of its evidence and reasoning.
